individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper proposes LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). It replaces implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from user drags, enabling full-strength inversion without test-time optimization. The method uses a winner-takes-all displacement field, Gaussian-noise initialization for inpainting regions, and attention controls (background token replacement, identity-preserving token concatenation, and gated output merging). Experiments on DragBench show improved MD, VIEScore metrics, and user preference over existing drag-based editing baselines.
Strengths: Identifies a core bottleneck in drag-based editing (implicit point matching) and proposes a clean alternative using an explicit correspondence map, which is intuitive and well-motivated.

First drag-based editing method designed for MM-DiTs that works with full-strength inversion while avoiding test-time optimization; exploits the improved inversion and attention controllability of MM-DiTs.

Technical design is thorough: WTA fusion handles opposing drags, Gaussian-noise initialization improves inpainting, and multi-part attention control preserves background and identity while allowing text-guided semantic changes.
Comprehensive experiments on DragBench show consistent improvements over eight baselines in MD, SC, PQ, O, and human preference; ablations validate the contribution of each component.
Weaknesses: The paper overclaims novelty ('first') without verifying against concurrent or less-known MM-DiT drag-editing methods; only U-Net baselines are compared.

IF (LPIPS) is omitted, and VIEScore is an automated MLLM metric that may not fully capture editing quality; the reported standard deviations are small but no significance tests are provided, and MD differences with DragText are marginal (21.49 vs 21.51).

The method depends on the specific FLUX.1 Krea-dev base model and UniEdit-Flow inversion; the transferability to other MM-DiTs or U-Nets is not demonstrated beyond a small U-Net ablation of one component.
The method description is dense and some design choices (e.g., region partition, transition region definition, choice of activation timestep) appear ad-hoc and are not rigorously justified.
The paper does not discuss the computational cost of inversion or provide runtime comparisons; 'no TTO' does not necessarily mean efficient.
Failure cases are only in the appendix; limitations like overlapping drags and small displacements could be better analyzed in the main text.
Questions: How does the method handle the choice of feature points P? Is it uniform or density-based, and how sensitive are results to this choice?
What is the exact definition of the transition region R^trans? How is its width or extent determined, and how does it interact with background and destination regions?

The paper claims full-strength inversion, but latent initialization still warps z_T. Does full-strength inversion mean the denoising starts from pure noise? If so, how does the explicit map survive after many steps?
Why is the VIEScore used instead of IF? Could the omission of IF hide perceptual quality degradation, and why not report both?

The ablation shows that removing ID Pres. and Attn Refine causes a large drop (MD 21.49 to 56.49). Is the attention-similarity control from CharaConsist the only alternative, or could simpler schemes like direct token copying perform better?
What is the runtime of the method compared to FastDrag or DragText? Does the inversion process add significant overhead?
Limitations: The method inherits limitations of the base MM-DiT and the inversion algorithm; performance may degrade on other models.
Small drag distances are not handled reliably due to VAE compression and latent patching.
Overlapping or conflicting drags can still produce artifacts if activation timestep is too high.
The approach is evaluated only on DragBench; generalization to other datasets or types of images (e.g., faces, objects) is not explored.
The paper does not address potential biases in the base model (e.g., gender, race, cultural) that may affect edits.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers. It replaces implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from drag instructions, uses this map to drive attention control (background replacement, key/value concatenation for identity, gated output refinement), and thereby enables full-strength inversion without test-time optimization. The method is evaluated on DragBench against eight baselines, reporting improved drag accuracy (MD), VIEScore perceptual metrics, and human preference, along with ablations and demonstrations of text-guided and multi-round edits.
Strengths: Principled replacement of fragile attention-similarity matching with a deterministic correspondence map from drag instructions, addressing root instability and allowing full-strength inversion without TTO.
Strong empirical results on DragBench: best MD and VIEScore among compared methods, no TTO requirement, and 61.88% human preference in a pairwise user study.
Comprehensive ablations show contributions of WTA fusion, latent initialization, background preservation, and identity-preserving attention control; components also transfer to U-Net-based FastDrag.
Demonstrates new capabilities beyond prior drag editing, including text-guided inpainting, ambiguous drag resolution, and move/scale multi-round editing.
Weaknesses: The MD improvement over DragText is marginal (21.49 vs 21.51), and no statistical significance tests are provided; it is unclear whether the accuracy advantage is meaningful given DragText requires TTO.
User study is modest (20 participants, 32 cases) and reports only preference percentages with large variance, without inter-annotator agreement or significance testing.

The method largely combines existing components (WTA displacement, noise-based latent init, CharaConsist-style attention control) into an MM-DiT pipeline; the conceptual novelty is incremental and lacks theoretical analysis of why full-strength inversion remains stable.
Evaluation relies on GPT-4o VIEScore with an adapted SC instruction; no standard fidelity metric (LPIPS/IF) is reported, and the results may be sensitive to the evaluator and prompt design.
Efficiency claims are not quantified: no wall-clock or GPU-time comparison against TTO-based baselines is provided despite 'training-free' being a central advantage.
The dependence on UniEdit-Flow inversion is not analyzed; it is unclear whether the approach works with other MM-DiT inversion methods or how inversion quality affects results.
Questions: What are the wall-clock and GPU-memory costs compared to TTO-based baselines (e.g., GoodDrag, DragDiffusion) and to FastDrag/Inpaint4Drag?
How sensitive is LazyDrag to the choice of inversion method (UniEdit-Flow vs. FireFlow vs. RF-Edit), and would the attention-control design transfer directly?
Is the 0.02 MD difference between LazyDrag and DragText statistically significant, and how does MD distribute across single-drag vs. multi-drag DragBench cases?
How are the transition and inpainting regions exactly computed from the displacement field, and what happens when no additional text prompt is provided for large inpainting regions?
Why is CFG set to 1? Does 'text guidance' rely solely on the base model's text conditioning, and how much do positive prompts improve SC/PQ in the quantitative benchmark?
Limitations: The method can produce unnatural artifacts when target points overlap or when drag distances are very small (acknowledged in Appendix B.4).
Performance depends heavily on the underlying base model; improvements in foundation models would be needed for further gains.
The paper only evaluates on DragBench; generalization to other benchmarks, out-of-distribution images, or video editing is not demonstrated.
Potential societal impact of more capable drag-based editing (e.g., creation of misleading imagery) is not discussed or mitigated.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method designed for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). Instead of relying on implicit attention-based point matching, LazyDrag builds an explicit correspondence map from user drag instructions and injects it into attention control. This enables full-strength inversion without test-time optimization (TTO), while preserving identity and background, and supports text-guided edits to resolve ambiguous drags. The method is evaluated on DragBench against eight prior drag-editing baselines, reporting improvements in drag accuracy (MD), VIEScore metrics (SC, PQ, O), and human preference, along with ablations and analyses.
Strengths: The core idea of replacing fragile implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from drag instructions is novel and well motivated; it directly targets a known weakness of prior drag-editing methods.

LazyDrag is the first drag-based editing method built for MM-DiTs and the first to demonstrate full-strength inversion in this setting, removing TTO and enabling more natural inpainting and text-guided edits.
The method is training-free and applies attention control only to single-stream attention layers, making it relatively efficient and architecture-aware.

The WTA displacement field and Gaussian-noise latent initialization are sensible improvements over FastDrag, particularly for opposing drags and large uncovered regions, and are validated by U-Net ablations.
Quantitative results on DragBench are strong across MD, SC, PQ, and O, and are complemented by a human study with 20 participants; the ablations isolate the contribution of each component.
Weaknesses: The quantitative comparison is confounded by the base model: all baselines use U-Net diffusion backbones while LazyDrag uses FLUX.1 Krea-dev (MM-DiT), so the reported gains may largely reflect the superior base model rather than the proposed editing mechanism; no same-backbone drag-editing baseline is provided.

Background preservation via token replacement may be incomplete because background queries can still attend to modified key/value tokens from edited regions; no attention masking or quantitative analysis is provided to show that background is truly unchanged.

The evaluation relies on MD and GPT-4o-based VIEScore while deliberately omitting standard fidelity metrics like LPIPS/IF; no statistical significance tests are reported, and the user study covers only 32 cases.

Some claims are not systematically evaluated, including multi-round workflows with simultaneous move and scale operations and the reported text-guidance advantage; only qualitative examples are shown.

Reproducibility is limited because the method depends on proprietary FLUX.1 Krea-dev and UniEdit-Flow inversion, with no code release or detailed hyperparameters for point sampling and mask construction; the TTO-Req flag may also understate the per-image inversion/initialization cost.
Questions: How do you ensure that background tokens are truly preserved when background queries can attend to modified key/value tokens from the edited regions? Would an explicit attention mask from background to non-background tokens further improve background consistency?

Can you provide a same-backbone comparison, for example by adapting FastDrag or CharaConsist to FLUX/MM-DiT, to isolate the contribution of LazyDrag's attention-control design from the gain due to the stronger base model? Have you tested the full LazyDrag on a U-Net baseline?

What exactly is meant by 'full-strength inversion' in contrast to weakened inversion strength? Is the UniEdit-Flow inversion still a per-image test-time process, and how is it excluded from the TTO-Req flag?

How are the drag instructions converted into the VIEScore SC prompt, and is the GPT-4o evaluator provided with the same source/target point overlays for all methods? Could the higher PQ/O scores be explained mainly by FLUX's generally higher image quality rather than the proposed method?
For the DragText baseline, is it a combination of GoodDrag and DragText? How is text guidance controlled across methods to ensure a fair comparison?

How does the method behave when multiple drag instructions have overlapping destinations or when the number of instructions is large? The failure cases in Fig. 9 suggest sensitivity to activation timestep—can you quantify this across the full benchmark?
Limitations: The evaluation does not control for base-model strength, as all baselines use U-Net backbones while LazyDrag uses FLUX/MM-DiT; the reported SOTA may not transfer to other backbones.
Background preservation is not guaranteed by token replacement alone because attention can still mix information from edited and background tokens; no attention masking is used.
The method inherits limitations of the underlying VAE/latent patching, struggling with very small drag distances and occasionally producing unnatural artifacts when target points overlap.
The paper relies heavily on LLM-based evaluation (GPT-4o) without standard fidelity metrics or significance testing, and the user study is relatively small.
The approach is training-free but still requires per-image inversion and token caching; no runtime or memory comparison is reported against TTO-free baselines.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). It replaces implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from user drag instructions, which drives attention control via token replacement, concatenation, and gated output merging. This enables full-strength inversion without test-time optimization, supports text-guided editing and natural inpainting, and is evaluated on DragBench with quantitative metrics, ablations, and a user study.
Strengths: Novel and principled approach: explicitly using the drag-derived correspondence map to drive attention control in MM-DiTs, avoiding fragile implicit attention similarity matching.

Method design is thoughtful: winner-takes-all displacement fusion avoids averaging failures for opposing drags, and region-aware latent initialization with Gaussian noise improves inpainting and reduces repetitive artifacts.
Strong empirical results on DragBench: LazyDrag achieves the best overall scores in terms of SC, PQ, O, and user preference, with ablations demonstrating the contribution of each component.
Training-free and TTO-free, making the method efficient and practical for interactive editing.
Clear writing and well-structured pipeline figure, with extensive qualitative results and appendix details.
Weaknesses: Unfair backbone comparison: LazyDrag uses FLUX.1 Krea-dev (a strong MM-DiT), while all baselines are U-Net-based Stable Diffusion models, so the reported improvements may largely come from the base model rather than the proposed method. No same-backbone comparison is provided.

Marginal drag accuracy improvement: MD is 21.49 vs. DragText's 21.51, a difference of only 0.02, which is smaller than the reported standard deviations, so the claim of state-of-the-art drag accuracy is not statistically substantiated.
Evaluation relies on GPT-4o-based VIEScore, which may introduce model bias and reproducibility concerns; standard perceptual metrics such as LPIPS are not reported.
User study is limited: only 20 participants and 32 cases, and no significance testing is performed, while the preference standard deviation is high (19).
No runtime or memory overhead comparison is provided despite the TTO-free claim, so the efficiency benefit is not quantified.

Some design choices lack thorough justification or comparison, such as the transition-region self-concatenation in Eq. 4, the exclusive use of single-stream attention layers, and the activation timestep schedule.
Ablations replace removed components with possibly suboptimal alternatives (e.g., CharaConsist attention-similarity control), which may overstate the importance of the proposed matching.
Questions: Can the authors provide a controlled comparison with all methods running on the same base model (e.g., FLUX.1 Krea-dev or SDXL) to isolate the effect of the proposed attention controls from the backbone choice?
Is the 0.02 MD improvement over DragText statistically significant, and what is the per-image distribution of MD across DragBench?
What are the wall-clock inference times and GPU memory requirements of LazyDrag compared to FastDrag and TTO-based methods?
Why does Eq. 4 use the source point itself for transition regions? Does this not simply concatenate the current tokens with themselves, and what is the intended effect?
How is 'full-strength inversion' defined operationally, and what inversion settings (e.g., DDIM steps, CFG, inversion strength) are used for each baseline?
How sensitive are the results to the density of sampled feature points P and to the Voronoi partition boundaries?
Limitations: The comparison is not controlled for base model strength, making it difficult to attribute the performance gains to the proposed method.
The evaluation is restricted to DragBench and a single MM-DiT (FLUX.1 Krea-dev), leaving generalization to other MM-DiTs untested.
The paper discloses failure cases for overlapping target points and very small drag distances, but does not analyze robustness to handle/target selection or mask quality.
No runtime or memory measurements are provided, so the practical efficiency advantage over TTO-based methods is not quantified.
Potential negative societal impact: photorealistic drag editing could be misused for creating misleading images, and the paper does not discuss safeguards or mitigation strategies.
The study lacks statistical significance testing for the VIEScore differences and user preferences.

review.Summary: The paper introduces LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method designed for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). The core idea is to replace fragile implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from user drag instructions. This map is used to construct an initial latent and to drive attention controls, enabling edits under full-strength inversion without test-time optimization (TTO). The method supports drag and move/scale modes, unifies geometric control with text guidance, and performs well on DragBench, achieving state-of-the-art results on MD, semantic consistency, perceptual quality, and user preference.
Strengths: Novel combination: LazyDrag is the first drag-based editing method for MM-DiTs, and it replaces implicit point matching with an explicit correspondence map, removing the need for test-time optimization.

The technical pipeline is well-structured, with WTA-based displacement fusion, latent initialization with random noise for inpainting regions, and two-part attention control (token replacement/concatenation and gated output refinement). Ablations validate each component.
Strong empirical results: LazyDrag outperforms eight baselines on DragBench in MD, VIEScore (SC, PQ, O), and a user study, while requiring no per-edit optimization, which is practically appealing.

The method handles challenging multi-drag conflicts (e.g., opposing drags) via winner-takes-all fusion, and demonstrates the ability to combine drag with text guidance for semantically consistent edits such as inpainting and ambiguous-object placement.
The ablation study, including compatibility with U-Nets, provides useful insights into the importance of the proposed components.
Weaknesses: The central claim of 'full-strength inversion' is not rigorously defined or compared against the inversion strengths used by prior methods; no quantitative evidence directly demonstrates that this is the key factor behind the improvements.

The evaluation deviates from standard DragBench practice: IF (LPIPS) is intentionally omitted, and VIEScore is computed with GPT-4o, which may introduce model-specific biases and makes comparison with previously reported metrics difficult.

The identity-preservation mechanism for transition regions uses the position itself as its own source (tilde M(x)=x), which seems semantically weak; the blending schedule h_t is not specified, hindering reproducibility.
The method is built on a specific FLUX model with UniEdit-Flow inversion, but no experiments on other MM-DiT models are provided, leaving generalizability across architectures unclear.

No runtime or memory comparison is reported, despite emphasizing the advantage of being TTO-free; the proposed token concatenation and cached-token interactions may still incur computational overhead.
Questions: What exactly is 'full-strength inversion' in this context, and how does it differ from the inversion schemes used in baselines like DragDiffusion or GoodDrag? Can the authors provide a direct comparison of their inversion schedule versus a weakened-inversion variant to substantiate the claim?
How is the h_t decay schedule in Equation (8) chosen, and is it tuned per dataset or per example? What is the sensitivity of the method to different decay curves?

For transition regions, the correspondence source is set to x itself (tilde M(x)=x). Does this simply duplicate cached tokens at the same location, and if so, how does that contribute to identity preservation during inpainting?

How is MD computed exactly on DragBench? Is it based on learned feature motion, optical flow, or the final token positions, and does the GPT-4o-based VIEScore evaluation correlate well with human judgments for drag edits?
Could a direct comparison on the standard DragBench IF (LPIPS) metric still be provided as a sanity check, even if it is not highlighted in the main results?
Limitations: The method is sensitive to the activation timestep; too high a timestep can cause artifacts when multiple target points overlap, as shown in the failure cases.
Small drag distances are challenging due to VAE compression and latent patching, leading to slight positional shifts.
The quality of edits depends heavily on the underlying base model (FLUX), and the method has not been tested on other MM-DiT architectures.
Potential misuse for image manipulation/manipulation of real images is not discussed in the paper.

review.Summary: The paper proposes LazyDrag, a training-free drag-based image editing method for Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). It replaces implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from user drags, enabling full-strength inversion without test-time optimization. The method uses winner-takes-all displacement fusion, Gaussian-noise latent initialization for inpainting regions, and attention controls (background token replacement, identity-preserving token concatenation, gated output merging). Experiments on DragBench show improvements in MD, VIEScore metrics, and human preference over existing drag-editing baselines, with ablations validating each component.
Strengths: The core idea of replacing fragile implicit attention-based point matching with an explicit correspondence map derived from drag instructions is novel, well-motivated, and directly addresses a known instability of prior drag-based methods.
LazyDrag is the first drag-based editing method designed for MM-DiTs and demonstrates full-strength inversion without test-time optimization, making it more practical for interactive editing.

The technical design is thorough: WTA displacement fusion handles opposing drags, Gaussian-noise latent initialization improves inpainting of uncovered regions, and attention controls preserve background and identity while enabling text-guided semantic changes.
Comprehensive experiments on DragBench show consistent improvements over eight baselines in MD, SC, PQ, O, and human preference, with ablations supporting the contribution of each proposed component.
The method is training-free and TTO-free, and the ablation study includes a transfer of one component to a U-Net baseline, demonstrating some generality.
Weaknesses: The quantitative comparison is confounded by the base model: LazyDrag uses the strong FLUX.1 Krea-dev MM-DiT, while all baselines are U-Net-based Stable Diffusion models, so reported improvements may largely reflect the base model rather than the proposed editing mechanism; no same-backbone comparison is provided.

The drag accuracy improvement over DragText is marginal (MD 21.49 vs 21.51, a difference of 0.02), and no statistical significance tests are provided; the claim of state-of-the-art drag accuracy is not strongly substantiated.
Evaluation relies on GPT-4o-based VIEScore and omits standard fidelity metrics such as LPIPS/IF; the user study is limited (20 participants, 32 cases) and lacks significance testing.

The method's dependence on the specific FLUX.1 Krea-dev model and UniEdit-Flow inversion raises concerns about generalizability to other MM-DiTs or inversion methods; no experiments on other MM-DiTs are provided.
Despite emphasizing the TTO-free advantage, no runtime, wall-clock, or GPU memory comparisons are reported, so the efficiency benefit is not quantified.

Some design choices (e.g., transition-region definition, activation timestep schedule, blending schedule h_t) appear ad-hoc and are not rigorously justified; the reported failure cases (overlapping targets, very small drag distances) are only placed in the appendix.
Questions: Can the authors provide a controlled comparison with all methods using the same base model (e.g., FLUX.1 Krea-dev or SDXL) to isolate the effect of the proposed attention controls from the backbone choice?
Is the 0.02 MD improvement over DragText statistically significant, and what is the per-image distribution of MD across DragBench?
What are the wall-clock inference times and GPU memory requirements of LazyDrag compared to TTO-free and TTO-based baselines?

How is 'full-strength inversion' defined operationally, and how does it compare to the inversion strengths used by prior methods? Could a weakened-inversion variant of LazyDrag be tested to substantiate the claim?
Why are standard fidelity metrics like LPIPS/IF omitted? Can these be reported as a sanity check, even if not the main metric?
How sensitive are the results to the choice of inversion method (UniEdit-Flow vs. others) and to the density/placement of sampled feature points P?
Limitations: The evaluation does not control for base-model strength, making it difficult to attribute the performance gains solely to the proposed method.
The method inherits limitations of the underlying VAE/latent patching, struggling with very small drag distances; overlapping target points can cause artifacts depending on the activation timestep.
Generalization to other MM-DiT architectures, datasets beyond DragBench, or video editing is not demonstrated.
The reliance on a proprietary base model (FLUX.1 Krea-dev) and inversion method may hinder reproducibility if no code is released.
Potential negative societal impacts of more capable drag-based editing (e.g., creation of misleading photorealistic images) are not discussed or mitigated.
